This study was followed by the MTEP 11 that included the first tranche of MVP projects. The MVP portfolio includes projects distributed throughout MISO’s footprint at the time and what is today the MISO Midwest subregion. MISO defines the qualifying criteria, benefit metrics, and cost allocation methods for MVP projects in its OATT (MISO 2024a). The underlying principle for MVP regional cost allocation is the assumption that MVP projects provide regional benefits in excess of costs. To qualify for MVP cost allocation, projects must meet at least one of three criteria roughly aligned with providing public policy, economic, and reliability benefits15: 1. Public policy: Reliably and economically deliver energy under the constraints of existing state and federal energy policy mandates, laws, and regulatory requirements. 2. Economic: Provide multiple types of economic benefits across multiple pricing zones. Benefit-to-cost ratio must exceed 1.0. 3. Reliability: Address at least one reliability issue in violation of a NERC or local utility standard and provide at least one economic benefit that provides value across multiple pricing zones. The MISO Board approved the MVP portfolio in 2011 under Criterion 1 because the projects helped MISO states meet their renewable portfolio standards.16 15 Additional tariff requirements for MVPs include projects must be evaluated as a portfolio, have a minimum cost of $20 million, be at least 100 kV, and provide benefits that are at least as much as costs (B/C ratio of 1.0) for projects selected under criteria 1 and 3. The tariff also specifies benefits to be looked at over a 20-year time frame and allows MISO to develop other benefits to evaluate MVP portfolios. 16 The MVP cost allocation scheme was adjudicated, but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit upheld FERC’s order approving MISO’s cost allocation for MVP projects in Illinois Commerce Commission v. MISO calculates the benefits of the portfolio, including production cost savings, reduced cost of meeting operating and planning reserve requirements, reduced transmission line losses, and deferred investments in future baseline reliability upgrades. These benefits are calculated for each cost allocation zone, aligned roughly with state boundaries, to show how costs and benefits are distributed throughout the region. Two Triennial Reviews have taken place in 2014 and 2017 to recalculate the benefit-to-cost ratio for the MTEP 11 MVP portfolio.
